title: Contentment with little
hook: a full cart that never checks out, and a one-sentence definition of wealth

segments.voice: Yesterday, loving for others, and your line: love it for them. Did someone's good news get a warm word from you? Today, a different kind of being rich. Day one thousand three hundred fifteen.

An online cart, full, never checked out. A closet with the tags still on. A search at three in the morning for something nobody needed at noon. Sometimes the wanting doesn't end when the package arrives; it moves on to the next thing. The Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, put a definition of wealth into one sentence. In Sahih al-Bukhari, in paraphrase: richness isn't having a great many things; real richness is richness of the soul. Today: being rich on the inside, and the word for it.
screen: `A CART THAT NEVER CHECKS OUT.` → `THE WANTING MOVES ON.` → `RICHNESS OF THE SOUL.`

segments.voice: The word is qana'ah: contentment, being satisfied with what you've been given. The soul in the hadith is nafs, the same word this path has used for the self that wants and wants. So the hadith moves wealth off the shelf and into the self. Two people can own exactly the same things. One feels poor, because the wanting runs ahead. The other feels rich, because it doesn't. Second, qana'ah isn't a vow to have nothing. In Sahih Muslim, the Prophet says, in paraphrase: successful is the one who has submitted, been given enough to live on, and been made content by Allah with what He gave. Enough. Not nothing. Third, a way to train it. Also in Muslim, in paraphrase: look at those below you, not at those above you; that way you won't belittle Allah's blessings on you. Look down the ladder, not up. A phone feed tends to run the other way. Fourth, a story of someone who missed it. In surah al-Kahf, a man with two rich gardens walks into his own grounds and says he doesn't think any of this will ever perish. His companion asks him, in paraphrase: when you entered your garden, why didn't you say, what Allah wills; there is no strength except in Allah? Ma sha' Allah. You may hear it said over good things: a new baby, a new house, a friend's success. It's a small tool of contentment. It hands the good thing back to the One who gave it. Qana'ah isn't wanting nothing. It's being able to stop at enough.
screen: `NAFS: WEALTH MOVES INTO THE SELF.` · `ENOUGH, NOT NOTHING.` · `LOOK DOWN THE LADDER, NOT UP.` · `THE TWO GARDENS: MA SHA' ALLAH.`

segments.voice: The practice: enjoy what you have. Settle, and breathe. Look around, or picture your room. Choose one thing you already own and haven't really looked at in a while. A mug. A coat. A window. A pair of shoes that still work. Look at it the way you'd look at something you just unwrapped. Notice what it does for you every day without asking anything back. If you pray, you can say quietly, ma sha' Allah, or alhamdulillah. If not, just stay with the thing, and with the word enough. The bell holds the time.
Qana'ah. Contentment: richness of the soul, enough given and enough accepted, without the wanting running ahead. Today's word.

Your line: rich in the soul. Today, before you buy or scroll for something new, use one thing you already have, on purpose, and enjoy it. Tomorrow, excellence in all things. Day one thousand three hundred fifteen.

howItsDone: Muslims cultivate qana'ah by thanking Allah for what they have, saying ma sha' Allah over good things, and following the hadith's advice to look at those with less rather than those with more.

fork.setup: a man walks into his two gardens, sure none of it will ever perish. his companion says there were words he should have said on the way in. what were they?
options: these are mine; I earned every one.
what Allah wills; there is no strength except in Allah.
nothing; it's better to stay quiet.
fork.reveal: al-Kahf: ma sha' Allah, la quwwata illa billah. the words hand the gardens back to their Giver. he didn't say them, and the gardens were ruined.

original.note: Arabic: contentment, being satisfied with what one has.

trapdoor: what you thought: contentment means not wanting anything.
what it means: qana'ah is stopping at enough: richness of the soul, given enough and made content with it.
what a scholar hears: Bukhari 6446's ghina al-nafs beside Muslim 1054's 'given enough': contentment is not poverty but a self that isn't chasing.
